summary:
**AgroOrbit** es una herramienta web creada para el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, dentro del desafío "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data". Está pensada para el este de San Luis, Argentina, una zona de transición donde llueven unos 790 mm anuales pero la atmósfera demanda más de 1.200 mm. Según el año, los lotes se comportan como húmedos o semiáridos. Por eso las rotaciones tradicionales, como soja y maíz con suelo desnudo en invierno, dejan al productor sin margen en años secos.

La aplicación diagnostica el lote con datos de la NASA (clima, humedad del suelo, verdor, relieve y temperatura superficial). Compara la rotación actual con seis alternativas mediante un puntaje de 0 a 100 que se explica por agua, suelo, riesgo, ingreso y sostenibilidad. El ranking se ajusta según las prioridades del usuario y se pueden simular escenarios como sequía, olas de calor o lluvias intensas. También arma un calendario por campaña, explica el efecto de cada cultivo sobre el suelo y emite alertas, con un mapa de lluvia animado. Incluye un modo simple para huertas.

Usa NASA POWER, SMAP, MODIS, HLS, ECOSTRESS, SRTM, GPM/IMERG y GIBS, combinados con SoilGrids y Open-Meteo. Cada dato indica fuente, fecha y si es observado, modelado o estimado. No reemplaza a un ingeniero agrónomo.
details:
INTRODUCTION

We are Los Tijuan, a team of students willing to work on solutions and to learn. This report presents our project for the challenge “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” of the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. We chose to focus it on agriculture because we believe that farm production and the conservation of natural resources are vitally important topics that often receive less visibility than they deserve.

Also, as students, we identified crop planting as a concrete challenge that we could develop and solve effectively, putting technology at the service of those who work the land.

Planning planting is one of the most complex tasks of the agricultural cycle, since it requires making decisions in the face of a changing climate. To address this problem in a comprehensive way, we focused our solution on managing four fundamental resources:

- Water: continuous monitoring of water availability and soil moisture to prevent losses from droughts or excess water.

- Soil and Land: care for the health of the terrain, erosion prevention, and promotion of vegetation cover to maintain fertility.

- Climate and Atmosphere: monitoring of temperatures, evapotranspiration, and weather variations to anticipate risks such as frosts or dry spells.

- Crops and Sustainability: comparative evaluation of crop rotation options to balance profitability with care for the ecosystem.

Although environmental and climate information exists, it is usually presented in complex formats. For this reason, we set out to translate it into clear and direct language for the farmer.

To meet this need, we developed AgroOrbit, an interactive web page that processes open NASA satellite data (on climate, soil moisture, vegetation, and terrain) and turns it into recommendations that are simple to apply. In AgroOrbit, users can outline their land directly on the map, define their production priorities, and compare different planting alternatives.

It is important to emphasize that AgroOrbit was created as a support and preliminary diagnostic tool; it does not aim to replace the advice of an agronomist or substitute for laboratory soil analysis.

In the following sections we present the objective of the project, how the platform works and how we process NASA satellite data, and we close with the recommendations, the final assessment, and proposals for its further development.

OBJECTIVE

General objective: to develop AgroOrbit, a decision-support tool that integrates NASA Earth observations with local information on soil, crops, and production priorities, in order to compare rotation strategies that strengthen soil health, optimize water use, and increase the resilience of agricultural systems to a changing climate.

Specific objectives:

- Characterize the agroclimatic conditions of each field plot from long-term series: climate and evapotranspiration with NASA POWER, soil moisture with SMAP, vegetation vigor with MODIS and Landsat HLS, thermal stress with ECOSTRESS, and elevation and slope with SRTM.

- Evaluate crop alternatives for the rotation according to their contribution to soil fertility and structure, their water demand, and their fit with the growing season and the user’s priorities, complemented with forecasts (Open-Meteo) and soil estimates (SoilGrids).

- Ensure the traceability and transparency of the information, showing on screen the source, the date, and the nature of each data point (observed, modeled, estimated, or assumed), and labeling soil nutrients as estimates to be validated with laboratory analysis.

- Deliver interpretable and actionable recommendations to farmers and agronomists that reduce exposure to water scarcity, erosion, nutrient depletion, and extreme weather events.

DEVELOPMENT

The climate no longer behaves as it used to, and those who farm feel it first. Rains arrive at different times, temperatures change more intensely, and droughts or frosts can appear when least expected. High-precision satellite information to understand these changes exists and is public, but it is usually hidden in complex scientific websites that are hard to navigate. As a result, many small and medium-sized farmers end up making decisions “by eye” or with outdated data, which causes economic losses when an unexpected weather event occurs and leads to the gradual degradation of the land.

In the face of that uncertainty, we designed AgroOrbit, a tool built to support those who work the land, from a large farm to a small family garden, and understandable both to agronomists and to people without technical training:

- Engineer users (agronomists and advisors): they seek precision and technical backing. The platform offers them detailed reports, shows the exact origin of each data point, and allows them to simulate different risk scenarios.

- Non-engineer users (farmers and home gardeners): they need quick and simple answers. The website turns difficult data into color bars, clear weather alerts, and direct advice on what to look after on their land (water, soil, or climate).

AgroOrbit does not aim to replace the experience of those who farm, but to organize information so that this experience can be applied at the best moment. In this way, it works as a meeting point between science and everyday work in the field.

To evaluate each field plot comprehensively, the platform organizes the analysis around four key resources: Water, Soil, Climate, and Crops. To monitor each one, we selected open NASA satellite sources, which ensure global, reliable, and up-to-date data. The SMAP, MODIS, Landsat HLS, and ECOSTRESS data are obtained through the AppEEARS service [6].

Climate: we incorporate NASA POWER [5], which provides daily series of precipitation, temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation. With them we calculate evapotranspiration (FAO-56 method [1]) and characterize climate zones through the aridity index (2015-2025). This makes it possible to understand the historical behavior of the place, see how it has changed, and detect in time whether a season shows extreme deviations from normal averages.

Water: we integrate NASA SMAP, which provides soil moisture information. The direct satellite measurement corresponds to the surface layer, and its modeled product makes it possible to estimate the water available in the root zone. Its value lies in identifying water stress and warning of droughts or excess moisture before the damage is visible on the plants. This helps to size irrigation better and avoid overwatering, protecting an increasingly valuable resource.

Soil: we use NASA SRTM [3], which provides the elevation and slope of the terrain. The slope of the plot determines how water runs off during heavy rains, which makes it possible to calculate the risk of water erosion and loss of topsoil.

Crops: we use the vegetation indices from MODIS (NDVI) and Landsat HLS, which measure green biomass density and plant vigor by sectors of the plot, and ECOSTRESS, which detects thermal stress in the plant canopy. These tools make it possible to analyze the behavior of vegetation cover during fallow periods and compare rotation options to balance production with land conservation.

To compare rotations, AgroOrbit combines the diagnosis of each resource with the production priorities defined by the user (for example, saving water, protecting the soil, or balancing profitability) and evaluates each alternative according to its contribution to soil fertility and structure, its water demand, and its fit with the growing season.

In addition, the platform shows the day’s satellite imagery, cloud cover, and animated rainfall maps through NASA GIBS [4] (MODIS and GPM/IMERG). We clarify that the precipitation used in the calculations comes from NASA POWER, while IMERG is used only to visualize rainfall across the territory. As a complement, we use sources that do not come from NASA: Open-Meteo [8] for the forecast of the coming days, SoilGrids [2] to estimate soil properties, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim [7] for searching localities and for the base map.

We decided to focus development and testing on the province of San Luis, Argentina, because of its agroclimatic variability, marked by periods of drought, frost risk, and soils vulnerable to water erosion. Working in a nearby and familiar territory allowed us to compare satellite measurements with the reality observed in local fields, adjust the algorithms, and help ensure that the recommendations are accurate for the area. In addition, since many producers in the region do not have tools to process complex spatial information, the platform brings this data closer in a simple three-step format, useful both in family gardens and in commercial farms. Using San Luis as the initial validation environment also allowed us to design a modular structure, ready to be extended to other provinces.

To guarantee transparency, AgroOrbit labels the origin of each data point on screen: Observed (real measurements from satellites or weather stations), Modeled (calculations and indices from the platform), Estimated (projections based on historical trends), and Assumed (parameters entered by the user to evaluate scenarios). Soil nutrients are not measured by any satellite: they are estimated with agronomic rules based on what the person enters, and they are always labeled “estimated: validate with soil analysis”, so they require laboratory confirmation before any investment.

The user’s journey is simple and consists of three steps:

1. They outline their land on the map.

2. They obtain the satellite diagnosis of the four key resources (Water, Soil, Climate, and Crops) and identify their points of vulnerability.

3. They define their production priorities and compare the best rotation options.

Each informed decision becomes a small act of care: for the crop, for the pocket of the person who grows it, and for the environment that sustains it. The final recommendations and the final assessment are presented in the conclusion.

CONCLUSION

AgroOrbit’s final recommendations

Based on the satellite diagnosis of the four key resources (Water, Soil, Climate, and Crops), AgroOrbit recommends:

- Prioritizing rotations that provide cover and fertility on plots with slopes or risk of water erosion.

- Choosing crops suited to the water availability of the plot, avoiding those with high water demand when soil moisture is low.

- Adjusting planting to the climate risks of the area, such as frosts and dry spells.

- Validating nutrients with laboratory analysis and consulting an agronomist before investing, since AgroOrbit is a support and preliminary diagnostic tool.

The final assessment of the project

AgroOrbit achieved its main purpose: to translate open NASA satellite data, which is difficult to interpret, into clear and actionable information, with full transparency about the source, date, and nature of each data point. It serves both agronomists, with detailed reports and traceability, and farmers, with alerts and direct advice. Validation in San Luis allowed us to adjust the algorithms and build a modular structure. Its main limitation is that soil nutrients are not measured by satellite, so they are estimated and require laboratory confirmation.

Proposals for improvement and extension to other provinces

We propose incorporating soil analyses uploaded by the user, deepening the evaluation of crops with local pest data and market prices, and adding automatic alerts and a version optimized for mobile phones with poor connectivity. Thanks to its modular design, AgroOrbit can be extended to other provinces by recalibrating the agroclimatic parameters of each region and validating the results with local producers and technicians, as was done in San Luis.

The expected impact is a more resilient agriculture, able to adapt to a changing climate without losing sight of caring for the environment: better-prepared crops, more conscious use of water, and healthier soils. AgroOrbit seeks to make knowledge arrive on time and within reach of those who sow, irrigate, observe, and wait, turning data into concrete support to keep farming with hope, responsibility, and a future.

REFERENCES

[1] Allen, R. G., Pereira, L. S., Raes, D., & Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration: Guidelines for computing crop water requirements (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56). Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

[2] ISRIC – World Soil Information. (n.d.). SoilGrids [Data set]. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://rest.isric.org/soilgrids

[3] NASA Earthdata. (n.d.-a). Common Metadata Repository (CMR): SRTM catalog and downloads [Data set]. NASA. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov

[4] NASA Earthdata. (n.d.-b). Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS): MODIS imagery and GPM/IMERG precipitation [Data set]. NASA. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://gibs.earthdata.nasa.gov

[5] NASA Langley Research Center. (n.d.). NASA POWER: Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources [Data set]. NASA. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://power.larc.nasa.gov

[6] NASA Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center. (n.d.). AppEEARS: Application for Extracting and Exploring Analysis Ready Samples (SMAP, MODIS, Landsat HLS, and ECOSTRESS products) [Data set]. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://appeears.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov

[7] Nominatim. (n.d.). Nominatim: Geocoding with OpenStreetMap data [Software]. OpenStreetMap. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org

[8] Open-Meteo. (n.d.). Open-Meteo weather forecast API [Software]. Retrieved November 15, 2026, from https://open-meteo.com
